title: Parsing
text: Pattern sixteen: parsing a text feed. Every price and quantity arrives as characters, and the parser runs on every single message. The general version allocates and consults the locale; the hot path reads digits straight into integer ticks.

title: The general version
text: The task: turn a line like this into a symbol, a price and a quantity. The general version wraps the line in a stringstream, splits it with getline, and converts with stod and stoi. It's short, it's standard, and it throws on bad input. The other common answer is a regex, which reads even better.

title: What it costs
text: Here's what each line costs. Constructing the stringstream sets up a stream buffer and a copy of the global locale. The line is copied into it, and lines of 16 characters or more don't fit the small-string buffer: 0.8 allocations per line here. getline copies each field into a string, and stod calls strtod, which follows the C locale and also parses exponents, hex and infinity. The regex version allocates three times per line, and walks an automaton. And the result is a double, so pattern fifteen's problems start right here.

title: The hot path version
text: The hot path takes a string view, and returns false instead of throwing. It finds the two commas, and the symbol is a view into the buffer, not a copy. The price is a digit loop straight into integer ticks, at most two decimals, with no double in between. The quantity uses std::from_chars: no locale, no allocation, no exceptions. It's strict by design: exponents, spaces and a third decimal are rejected, because the feed spec forbids them. On two hundred thousand random lines, it gives the same results as the general version.

title: Measured
text: Measured on a shared 4 vCPU cloud VM, four thousand lines, pinned to one core. stringstream, getline and stod: about 300 nanoseconds per line, 100 per field. The regex: 730 nanoseconds at best, and its median more than doubled when the box got busy. from_chars with a double price: 27. The digit loop into ticks: 19 nanoseconds per line, about 6 per field, fifteen times faster than the stream, with zero allocations. At a million messages a second, that's 30 percent of a core, against 2.

title: The rule
text: The general parsers are right for config files, command lines, CSV reports and tests: rare, varied input, where a clear error message matters most. On a feed handler, the format is fixed by the venue's spec. So state it: no allocation, integer ticks, reject anything off spec, and report errors as values. The rule: parse the bytes you were promised, straight into the type you'll use.
